In this lesson you will learn about the AC motor.
INTRODUCTIONM
AC motors, just like DC motors, convert electrical energy into mechanical energy.
AC motors use AC or Alternating Current as an electrical input source.
Because of an AC input signal, AC motors are much different in their theory of operation than the DC motor.

LESSON MENU
AC motors, just like DC motors, are classified as continuous devices. Rotating Machinery Motor Incremental Continuous DC AC
DISCUSSION
As you know, DC motors have certain operating characteristics. Motor Characteristics 1. High Starting Torque 2. Speed Control Capabilities 3. Large Starting Current
When an application requires one or more of these features, a DC motor is usually used.
When these features are not required, the AC motor is usually used.
Since AC power is used in every home and offices worldwide, the AC motor is the most popular device. AC Supply
Based on their construction, AC motors can be classified into three categories: universal, induction and synchronous.
The universal motor is essentially a DC motor with AC applied.
Synchronous motors are either large horse power or special application devices, seldom found by electronics technicians.
Applications for AC induction motors include: machines, pumps, spindles and clocks.
AC and DC motors are classified as what type?
Induction and synchronous motors are only classified as AC motors.
TRY AGAIN!
All motors require the same basic criteria for motor action to occur.
There are, however, some major differences between the DC and AC motor construction.
AC motor rotors do not have turns of wire connected externally to a voltage source through a commutator assembly.
AC rotors (inductor type) have a distinct appearance and are often referred to as squirrel cage rotors.
The squirrel cage rotor is simpler and less expensive to manufacture than the DC rotor.
The squirrel cage rotor requires no commutator or brush assembly. This reduces cost, maintenance and sparking.
The stator of an AC motor is similar to the stator of a DC motor.
In both motor types, the field windings are placed on pole pieces to generate a magnetic field.
Which part listed below is used in AC motors only?
A stator is common to both DC and AC motors and works with the rotor to generate motor action.
TRY AGAIN!
The commutator and brushes are common to a DC motor only...
TRY AGAIN!
Since an AC induction motor's rotor has no commutator, brushes or applied voltage source, it cannot generate a field.
The only field induced in an AC motor is a result of the windings around the pole pieces.
If an AC induction motor has only one field in the stator, how can motor action occur?
To understand AC motor action, let's use 3 moving magnets:
Assume that the outside magnets (stator magnets) rotate and that the distance between the two magnets is small.
Attracted forces between the two magnets cause the rotor magnet to follow.
The rotor will rotate around the pivot point.
If the rotor magnet keeps pace with the stator magnets, then the magnets are said to be synchronized.
If this rotation could be maintained, motor action would then exist.
An actual AC inductor motor is slightly more complicated than three moving magnets.
The stators of an AC induction motor are fixed and do not rotate.
The rotor of an AC induction motor is not a magnet.
To understand an actual AC induction motor, consider two sine waves, 90
The two sine waves are applied to different pole pairs (2 poles) of the induction motor.
If you consider the stator windings to be purely inductive, stator currents will also be 90 degrees out of phase.
If you consider the stator windings to be purely inductive, stator currents will also be 90 degrees out of phase.
DEFINITION
These stator currents (not voltages) cause pulsating magnetic fields that rotate in a circle around the rotor.
Initially, 1 is at its zero crossing point, while 2 is at maximum.
Since 2 current is maximum, a magnetic field is developed across the poles connected to 2.
At line T1, 2 is zero and 1 is maximum. This corresponds to maximum 1 current and minimum 2 current.
Since 1 current is maximum, a magnetic field is developed across the poles connected to 1.
At time T2, 1 is zero and 2 now has it's maximum negative value.
Because 2 is negative, it corresponds to a reversed polarity magnetic field on the connected stator poles.
At time T3, 2 is zero and 1 is at it's maximum negative value.
Because 1 is negative, it corresponds to a reversed polarity magnetic field on the connected stator poles.
At time T4, each waveform has completed one cycle and the process begins again.
The changing amplitude of the waveforms cause the stator magnetic fields to constantly expand and contract, as well as rotate.
Because of expanding and contracting stator magnetic fields, rotor current is induced. This is due to induction.
This is how the motor derives it's name, the AC induction motor.
All squirrel cage rotors have induced current flow through the connecting rods via the shorting rings.
The induced currents in the rotor will induce a magnetic field in the rotor.
The induced magnetic field in the rotor is attracted to the stator magnetic field.
As the stator field changes, the rotor field follows due to this attraction.
Due to the attraction of the stator field and the rotor field, motor action occurs.
What induces current in the rotor of an induction motor?
Stator voltage is related to stator current only. The voltage cannot induce a rotor current.

The stator magnetic field rotates from pole pair to pole pair.
How fast the stator magnetic field rotates is known as the Field Speed or Field RPM.
Field RPM can easily be calculated. ield RPM Formula 60 () Field RPM = N = Frequency of Input (Hz) N = # of Pole Pairs
If the input sine wave has a frequency of 60 Hz and the motor has 4 stator poles, the field RPM equals 1800. Back: P1580

Due to magnetic attraction, the rotor attempts to follow the stator (in rotation).
The rotor's RPM always lags behind the stator's magnetic field RPM.
This is called slip RPM because the rotor slips or lags behind the stator magnetic field.
How fast the rotor actually rotates is termed shaft speed..
Shaft RPM can be calculated since it is the difference between the Field RPM and the Slip RPM. Shaft RPM Formula Shaft RPM = Field RPM - Slip RPM 60 () Shaft RPM = - Slip RPM N

Since the rotor is always trying to catch up or synchronize with the stator field RPM, the field RPM is commonly called the Synchronous Speed of the armature. eld RPM = Synchronous Speed 60 () = frequency of input (Hz) Field RPM = N N = # of Pole Pairs

As an example of shaft speed, assume the motor's synchronous speed is 1800 RPM with a slip speed of 100 RPM. How fast is the motors output shaft spinning? Shaft RPM Formula Shaft RPM = Field RPM - Slip RPM 60 () Shaft RPM = - Slip RPM
Since synchronous speed is field RPM and slip speed is slip RPM, the motor's output shaft (shaft RPM) is rotating at
1700 RPM. AFT RPM = FIELD RPM - SLIP RPM = Synchronous Speed - Slip Speed = 1800 RPM - 100 RPM Motors Output Shaft = 1700 RPM

Looking at an AC induction motor, indicates an inductor (stator) very close to a conductor (rotor).
Since there is no electrical connection between the stator and rotor, the magnetic field of the stator induces voltage in the rotor coils.
This is identical to transformer action. condary (Rotor) Primary Primary Secondary (Stator) (Stator) (Rotor) Electrical
Sometimes the stator is called the primary and the rotor is called the secondary.
An equivalent electrical drawing of the stator and rotor is a step down transformer.
A step down transformer has less voltage and more current on the secondary than the primary.
The primary to secondary winding ratio will have a significant effect on current.
Compared to its input current, the output current of a motor is larger.
Remember, torque and current are proportional. The higher the current, the higher the torque.
Rotor current depends on the relative motion between the stator's magnetic field and the conductor (rotor).
If the rotor is locked (no rotation), there is maximum relative motion between the rotating stator field and the conductor (rotor).
This produces maximum current and maximum torque.
If the rotor is turning at the same RPM as the stator's magnetic field, there is no relative motion between the rotating stator field and conductor (rotor).
No current is produced and the torque is zero.
This is an important concept when discussing loaded and unloaded AC motor characteristics.
